packs.title: Across the Water
packs.promise: Find patterns, small clues and a different pace across Macau.

q.s: Find a small pattern inside a busy square.
st: From an open edge of Senado Square, choose one dark paving band and follow it with your eyes until it bends or disappears. Stay still while looking.
Collect three relationships in words: a dark band beside a light one, a bend, and a place where the band meets an edge or leaves your view.
Look away and describe which way you think that band turns next. Look back to check. An obscured section can remain unknown.
Choose a second band and see whether your first description fits it too. Keep one match or difference.

q.s: Let one opening lead to another.
st: Choose an open visitor viewpoint through a doorway toward another space. Notice what the first frame reveals and what it conceals.
Write three brief lines for an imagined silent visitor: what they notice before the opening, what becomes visible through it, and where they choose to stop.
Give each line one observed detail of space, such as a narrowing passage or a patch of sky. If the third space is hidden, make the stopping point the end of your story.
Read the lines in reverse order. Decide whether the return changes the mood and give your original sequence a title.

q.s: Test what an opening allows you to see.
st: From public paths in the fortress grounds, find three different viewing edges: a gap, a broad low edge and a corner or another safe boundary.
For each, collect a short description of what it lets you see. Decide which feels broadest and which directs your attention most narrowly.
If space allows, take two safe paces along one public path and compare that same opening again. If you stay still, compare two differently framed source photographs instead.
Read the fortress description and keep one observation about how a wall or opening shapes the view. Any proposed former function can remain a question.

packs.title: Between Barra & the Hill
packs.promise: Look closer along the lanes from Barra to St Augustine’s Square.

q.s: Match a visible detail with a practical job.
st: Find a model, object or image associated with carrying people or goods, one with moving a vessel, and one with finding or showing a way. One display may supply more than one role.
Assign each chosen detail to a job in short notes. Check the label where possible and leave an uncertain match as a question.
Imagine you could keep only two of the three in a tiny toolkit. Choose the two and explain what problem the missing one would leave.
Check one match against its display or the official permanent-exhibition description. Revise it if the evidence changes your choice.

q.s: Find the unit that makes a long front.
st: Choose one complete arch unit visible from the public area. Notice three component shapes in its opening, border or ornaments.
Look away and recall the three components in words. Then check the real arch or photograph to recover a missed detail.
Find the next unit with your eyes and test whether your description fits. Search for an end or corner where the repeat stops or turns.
Keep the component that best identifies this pattern and one way its ending differs.

q.s: Change a frame while keeping the place intact.
st: Choose an open visitor viewpoint including a courtyard, doorway or window. You can stay in one place.
Make four thumbnail sketches or four written frame descriptions: mostly bright area, mostly shade, their boundary, and the balance you prefer. Grey weather still offers lighter and darker surfaces.
Keep only light and surfaces you can see. Use shading or words instead of recording every ornament.
Compare the four frames, title your favourite and explain which framing choice changed the scene most.
